beliefs.practice: Read the DocumentDB connection string from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) at runtime and never commit the URI or any credentials to source control or logs; provide only a .env.example placeholder.
Use a single long-lived MongoClient instance per process (create one MongoClient and reuse it for all requests) rather than creating a new client per request or operation.
Ensure TLS/SSL is enabled for connections (require server certificate verification) and reject insecure connections; enforce tls=true/tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=false in connection options.
Configure reasonable connection pool and timeouts on the MongoClient (e.g., maxPoolSize tuned to app concurrency, set connectTimeoutMS and socketTimeoutMS) instead of relying on defaults.
Implement exponential backoff retries for transient network errors and throttling responses; specifically detect 429 (throttling) responses and respect any Retry-After header before retrying.
Make writes idempotent by using unique request identifiers and upserts (findOneAndUpdate with upsert or updateOne with upsert and $set) so repeated retries won’t create duplicates.
Create indexes on all fields used in predicates and sorts for hot queries (e.g., requestId, patientId, status, createdAt) and create compound indexes for filters+sort combinations to avoid COLLSCAN.

For vector-enabled queries, create and configure a dedicated vector index on the embedding field (explicitly specify index type and metric) and keep embedding dimensionality consistent across documents.

Precompute and store text embeddings (and normalize them if necessary) rather than computing on every query; store embeddings in a dedicated field and version the embedding schema if you change the encoder.
Limit document size: do not embed large binary or PDF blobs in documents; instead store large files in blob storage (Azure Blob) and include a reference (URL or id) in the DocumentDB document.

Use collection-level JSON Schema validation to enforce required fields and types for pre-auth requests and submission documents (e.g., require requestId, patientId, status, createdAt, embedding shape).
Use TTL indexes for ephemeral data (drafts, temporary caches) to automatically expire old documents instead of manual cleanup tasks.

When updating status and storing the final submission, prefer single-document atomic updates (updateOne with $set) or use a transaction only if you must update multiple collections atomically; keep transactions short.
Monitor queries and indexes using explain() and the server profiler; add indexes for high-frequency queries revealed by explain and remove unused indexes that waste RU/storage.
Instrument RU/throughput and latency metrics for the collection (or database) and adjust provisioned throughput or query patterns to avoid throttling—watch vector queries for high RU consumption.
Use least-privilege database credentials: create a dedicated DB user with only the required roles (readWrite on sample_healthcare_08) instead of using an admin/root account in the app.
Project only necessary fields in queries (use projection) when reading documents (e.g., exclude large fields like full clinical notes or embeddings when not needed) to reduce bandwidth and RU costs.

Write idempotent, resumable orchestrator logic: persist intermediate state (e.g., reviewResult, letterDraft) with timestamps so the orchestrator can resume or retry without duplication if interrupted.
Make seeding scripts idempotent: create collections and createIndex calls should be safe to run multiple times and should not drop production data; gate destructive operations behind explicit flags.

Avoid full-collection scans in aggregations: include $match early in pipelines, limit and paginate with range filters on indexed fields, and use $limit/$skip carefully to avoid large sorts without indexes.

For concurrent updates to the same submission, use optimistic concurrency control (e.g., a version number or updatedAt + conditional update) or findOneAndUpdate with a filter on the current version to prevent lost updates.

Ensure your MongoDB driver version is compatible with the server wire protocol (use a driver supporting MongoDB 7.0 features if you rely on 7.0 vector/search features) and pin the dependency in package.json.
When running tests, separate fast unit tests (mocking MongoClient) from integration tests that exercise the live DocumentDB cluster and gate live tests with environment variables or CI flags.
Avoid storing PHI in logs and redact sensitive fields before any diagnostic logging or error reports; ensure the app’s log retention and access controls meet privacy/regulatory requirements.

Set an appropriate readPreference (primary for strongly consistent reads used by the orchestrator when reading newly written submissions; secondaryPreferred for analytics or non-critical reads) to match consistency needs.
